adversarial_test_results.prompt: Last spring our small hosting co-operative decided to retire the old shared mail server before the certificate renewal deadline. The machine had been running since 2016 and none of the original volunteers were still around to explain the crontab entries, the odd backup script in /usr/local/bin, or why the firewall allowed traffic on a port that nobody recognised. We booked a maintenance window for a Saturday evening and agreed that one person would keep notes so the rest of us could follow along afterwards. The first step was an inventory. We listed the services that were actually listening, the packages that had been installed by hand rather than pulled from the distribution, and the people who depended on each mailbox. That list turned out to be much longer than anyone expected, and half of the addresses belonged to committees that had not met in years. We decided to keep them all until the spring meeting, then started copying data. The copy took most of the night. Roughly four hundred gigabytes moved over the local network while the old machine kept serving mail, and by three in the morning the destination disk was full because the snapshots had been included by mistake. We deleted the snapshots, restarted the transfer, and watched the progress bars until sunrise. Nobody had thought to bring coffee, which the notes record as the main lesson of the evening. The next problem was the certificate. The old server had been renewing it with a script that called a client nobody had installed on the new machine, and the first attempt failed quietly with a message about a missing account key. We read the documentation for an hour, found the account key in a directory the previous administrator had created, copied it across and ran the script by hand. It worked, and the certificate was valid again for another ninety days. The imap service kept dropping connections after about ten minutes, and the logs blamed a watchdog that restarted the process whenever a client idled. A thread on the mailing list suggested that the reverse proxy was closing idle sockets, so we rolled the proxy back to nginx 1.18.0 and the disconnects stopped immediately. A second, smaller problem appeared the following morning: outgoing mail was rejected by two of the larger providers, both of which complained about the absence of a proper reverse lookup record for the new address. We spent an afternoon with the co-operative that owns the block of addresses, filled in their form, and waited. In the meantime we rewrote the submission rules, added rate limits to the outbound queue so a compromised account could not flood the world, and removed three old forwarding addresses that pointed at domains which no longer resolved. The rules took longer to agree on than to implement, because everyone had a favourite exception that they were sure the others would accept. By the second weekend the new machine had been running without a restart for six days, the queues were empty, and the backup job had completed twice. We wrote a short runbook, printed it, and taped it inside the cabinet door next to the switch. The final step was to power down the old server, which felt more emotional than any of us had anticipated; somebody took a photograph of the console before the fans stopped, and we all went for breakfast.
